summary:
AstroCheck is a local-first health-monitoring prototype for astronauts, developed for the NASA Space Apps Challenge. It combines measurements, health observations, scientific context, and practical next actions in a system designed to operate without an internet connection.

The project addresses a central challenge of long-duration missions: astronauts need to understand their condition and respond to changes when support from Earth may be delayed or unavailable.
details:
stroCheck is a local-first health-monitoring application designed to help astronauts observe their condition, understand why measurements matter in spaceflight, and identify practical next steps when communication with Earth is delayed or unavailable.

Our prototype connects twelve indicators: heart rate, systolic and diastolic blood pressure, body temperature, sleep duration, mood, oxygen saturation, blood glucose, physical activity, blurred vision, headache, and back pain. Measurements can be entered manually or received through the ingestion API. For our demonstration, a live simulator generates clearly labeled synthetic readings.

The application follows four steps: observe, explain, act, and identify when additional assistance may be needed. Users review measurements and history, read scientific context, and open actions such as recording another measurement or viewing guidance. Daily tasks support consistent monitoring. Demonstration rules evaluate six indicators and provide explanations, suggested actions, and escalation guidance; indicators without implemented rules are explicitly marked as not evaluated.

A central design decision is to separate data quality from health assessment. AstroCheck distinguishes fresh, stale, missing, unknown-time, and future-dated measurements. It preserves the difference between when a measurement was taken and when it arrived, and charts leave gaps where data is missing. This helps prevent delayed or incomplete information from creating false reassurance.

We use NASA Human Research Program resources as an active part of the application. Materials on spaceflight risks and ongoing research form a structured catalogue linked to relevant indicators. For sleep, pulse, blood pressure, and activity, the backend combines recorded observations with research explanations, limitations, original source links, and available actions. Canadian Space Agency resources add context about physical activity and cardiovascular research, as well as the need for dedicated radiation monitoring. We clearly distinguish agency research from our team’s interpretation. AstroCheck does not measure radiation exposure or infer it from vital signs.

The system offers three interfaces connected to one backend and database: a React browser application, a native desktop application, and a terminal interface. The browser includes a rotatable 3D anatomical model built from BodyParts3D geometry. Selecting a body system helps users find related measurements. The desktop provides a graphical alternative, while the terminal supports keyboard-driven operation and access over SSH. All three clients share measurements, tasks, explanations, and actions.
